'''Peter John Stang''' (born November 17, 1941) is an American chemist and Distinguished Professor of chemistry at the [[University of Utah]]. He was the [[editor-in-chief]] of the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]'' from 2002 to 2020.<ref name="axial_2020">{{cite web |last1=Stanchak |first1=Jesse |title=Erick Carreira to Serve as Next JACS EIC |url=https://axial.acs.org/2020/09/03/erick-carreira-next-jacs-eic/ |website=ACS Axial |date=3 September 2020 |publisher=American Chemical Society |access-date=28 December 2020}}</ref><ref name="jacs_editors">{{cite web |title=Editors & Editorial Board |url=https://pubs.acs.org/page/jacsat/editors.html |website=Journal of the American Chemical Society |access-date=7 January 2021}}</ref>

==Biography==
[[File:Peter Stang - National Medal of Science, 2010.webm|thumb|Stang discusses his contributions to the field of chemistry, as well as his dedication to public service.]]
Peter Stang was born in [[Nuremberg, Germany]] to a German mother and Hungarian father. He lived in [[Hungary]] for most of his adolescence. In school, he took rigorous mathematics and science courses. At home, he made black gunpowder from ingredients at the drugstore, and developed a pH indicator from the juice of red cabbage that his mother cooked, and sold to his "fellow chemists".<ref name="nsf">{{cite web|title=Peter Stang -- National Medal of Science 50th Anniversary|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/medalofscience50/stang.jsp|website=National Science Foundation|access-date=14 April 2017}}</ref>

In 1956, when Stang was in the middle of his sophomore year in high school, he and his family fled the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956|Soviet invasion of Hungary]] and immigrated to [[Chicago, Illinois]]. Not speaking English, Stang failed his American history and English courses but scored at the top of his class in science and math.<ref name="nsf"/> His teachers were confused by his performance and gave him an IQ test. Stang was confused by the unfamiliar format of the test and scored a 78.<ref name="nsf"/> In spite of this, Stang was admitted to [[DePaul University]] and earned his undergraduate degree in 1963. He received his Ph.D. in 1966 from the [[University of California, Berkeley]].

After spending a year in as a [[NIH]] [[Postdoctoral]] Fellow at [[Princeton University]] with [[Paul Schleyer]], Stang joined the chemistry faculty at the [[University of Utah]] in 1969.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Stang|first1=Peter J.|title=From Solvolysis to Self-Assembly|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|date=2 January 2009|volume=74|issue=1|pages=2–20|doi=10.1021/jo801682d|issn=0022-3263|pmc=2736610|pmid=19111062}}</ref> He became dean of the [[University of Utah College of Science|College of Science]] in 1997, during which he established the [[John Warnock|John E. and Marva M. Warnock]] Endowed Chair in Mathematics, and oversaw construction and dedication of the new David M. Grant NMR Center in 2006. He stepped down as dean in 2007.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Harward|first1=Randy|title=News of the University|url=http://continuum.utah.edu/back_issues/2007spring/gazette.html|website=Continuum|publisher=University of Utah|access-date=13 April 2017|date=Spring 2007}}</ref>   He is a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]. He was editor-in-chief of the [[Journal of Organic Chemistry]] from 2000 to 2001. In 2013 he was awarded the [[American Chemical Society]] [[Priestley Medal]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Wilson|first1=Elizabeth K.|title=Peter J. Stang Named Priestley Medalist|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=23 July 2012|volume=90|issue=30|page=5|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i30/Peter-J-Stang-Named-Priestley.html|access-date=14 April 2017|doi=10.1021/cen-09030-notw1|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He served as editor in chief of the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]'' from 2002 to 2020, succeeded in 2021 by [[Erick M. Carreira]].<ref name="axial_2020" /><ref name="jacs_editors" />

==Research interests==

Stang's research has focused on designing, and synthesizing, small organic molecules which self-assemble into larger geometric shapes with potential applications as nano-devices, shape-selective catalysts, and molecular agents for separation by chelation and chromatography.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://iam.njtech.edu.cn/en/view.asp?id=90&class=37 |title=Prof. Peter J. Stang-Institute of Advanced Materials |access-date=2018-08-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804213930/http://iam.njtech.edu.cn/en/view.asp?id=90&class=37 |archive-date=2017-08-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://chem.utah.edu/directory/stang.php | title=Peter J. Stang - Department of Chemistry - the University of Utah | access-date=2018-08-09 | archive-date=2021-04-18 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210418114009/https://chem.utah.edu/directory/stang.php | url-status=dead }}</ref>
